newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai brokers expect smaller bonuses this year.
newsitem.headline: Thai brokers expect smaller bonuses this year.

text.p: Thai brokers expect to receive smaller annual bonuses this year due to declining volumes on the bearish stock exchange, now lingering at three-year lows.
Industry-wide bonus payments would average around three or four months' pay compared with last year's six, senior executives at brokerages told Reuters.
"What concerns brokers is trading volume," said Chartchai Parasuk, vice-president at National Finance and Securities, one of the larger local brokers.
"Volume of five to seven billion baht ($200-$250 million) a day is needed for the industry to break even and recently it has averaged three to four billion."
The value of trade during the first 11 months of 1996 was 1.237 trillion baht, down from 1.426 trillion baht in the same period of 1995, according to the Stock Exchange of Thailand.
"There are too many brokers and the pie is not big enough," Chartchai said.

Smaller securities brokers, without the support of a finance arm and more reliant on local trade, may not pay a bonus at all while foreign and larger local houses would probably keep payments at around last year's level, executives said.

"I think there are some smaller companies that will be struggling to pay any bonus at all. Retail trade has been most affected this year. There just hasn't been enough business," said one Thai securities manager.
In the first 11 months of 1996, retail buying was worth 663.66 billion baht, accounting for 53.64 percent of all trade on the market, a 22 percent decline over the year-earlier period.
"We will pay a bonus, but it has been a relatively difficult year and we can't compete with some of the bigger companies," said the managing director of a small Thai broker.

Overall industry profits have declined only marginally, to 14.225 billion baht in the first nine months of 1996 compared to 14.451 billion a year earlier, according to figures from The Multi-Credit Corporation.
That meant the chance of bigger local houses and their foreign affiliates matching last year's bonuses was better, company executives said.
"We have a reasonable bonus pool this year... Most of the brokers who depend on institutional business have done okay," said a country manager for a foreign broker.
"Generally their market share has increased because the retail side of the market has been hit hard... Some foreign firms pay bonuses according to regional profits," he said.

A 28 percent decline in the key SET index so far this year may have squeezed most investment banking department profits by hindering initial public offerings this year, executives said. But foreign buying had increased.

Buy orders from foreigners were up 1.13 percent in the first 11 months to 432.685 billion baht, accounting for 34.97 percent of market trading value compared to 27.87 percent over the equivalent period last year. (US$1 = 25 baht)
